Article Title: An ancient British farming craft faded after World War II; now 2,500 farmers want to revive 1,300km of mature hedgerows to help wildlife and reduce flooding
Article Text:
The art of hedge laying

It's seeing a revival and how. The ancient craft of hedge laying is back in trend among farmers as they are using the technique dating back to 18th and 19th centuries in order to boost wildlife, capture carbon and help tackle flooding. Hedge laying which restores and revives mature hedges to keep them fresh was among the four most popular categories of capital grants selected by farmers out of a total pot of £225m provided by the government this year to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside.The 2,500 farmers across England who applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using the craft that dates back to thousands of year will lay 1,300 km of mature hedgerows, if the grants are approved. According to Megan Gimber, the key habitats officer for the People's Trust for Endangered Species said that hedge laying was one of the most effective tools farmers had to respond to the climate crisis. “Hedge laying really stopped after the war, so it has been over a generation since it was a normal part of farm management and we have seen a huge decline in hedgerows as a result,” she said.“These grants will give 1,300km of potentially ancient hedges a new lease of life, to help plug the gap, and it is fantastic that it is such a popular grant application.”Mature, maintained hedgerows are a carbon sink that capture more carbon in every hectare than forests. They support thousands of species, provide shade for livestock, reduce soil erosion and slow down, absorb and store vast amounts of rainwater to help reduce flooding. “They are massively important,” said Stephen Budding, the chair of the National Hedgelaying Society. “The greatest biodiversity gain is from hedge laying older hedges. “Our members are seeing quite a surge in work, but I don’t think this would be happening without the government grants available.”Hedge laying involves cutting through the hedge stems almost completely, then laying them at an angle to the ground. Laying the branches down invigorates growth at the point where they have been cut, filling gaps in the hedges and restoring youth and freshness.The craft is done by hand by skilled layers, many of whom will also be competing next month at the National Hedgelaying Championships in Chipping Norton. It was extremely common until World War II, post which there was a massive shift toward industrialised farming, cheap manufactured fencing and also severe shortage of labour.Robert Rose, who farms 220 acres of grassland for beef cattle and arable fields at Rosewood Farm in Ellerton in Yorkshire’s Lower Derwent valley, is waiting for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) to approve his application for a grant to lay old blackthorn, newer hawthorn and ash and willow hedges across his farm. “We lay the hedges in a modern conservation style that retains more of the bushy growth for the benefit of nesting birds as well as stock proofing,” said Rose, who farms with his brother and wife.The trio planted new hedges about 20 years ago, but maintaining them is vital to keep them working to store carbon, support wildlife and retain water. “We taught ourselves how to do the laying, which was a bit of trial and error,” he said. “It is only recently that we have noticed how much other farmers are talking about hedge laying online, in community groups, it really seems to be taking off.” The grant Rose has applied for will aid him in laying about 50 metres of hedges along with planting new hedgerows and coppicing others. Peak hedge laying season starts in October and ends in February, so farmers like Rose are hoping for quick decisions from Defra. “There are so many benefits with hedge laying for wildlife, for livestock, for conservation. We see a lot more birds using the hedges and a lot more small mammals around the bottom of mature managed hedges,” said Rose.Along with grant requests for hedge laying, about 5,000 applications are for planting new hedges, representing approximately 2,500 km of new hedgerows. But these will not survive without management. The centre also discovered that 61% of the newly planted hedges surveyed existed as hedges in their 2007 survey, but had since been lost and required replanting.“Hedgerows are succession habitats, made up of trees and shrubby woody species, that naturally change over time,” said Gimber. “They require management to maintain the valuable mid-succession stage of bushy, low growth and prevent them developing into lines of trees.”“This government is putting its full weight behind farmers – giving them the funding, tools and opportunities they need to succeed. In July, we opened a new round of environmental land management capital grants with increased funding of up to £225m available to support investment in infrastructure that boosts productivity, strengthens resilience and supports environmental outcomes, which has now closed following strong uptake,” said a Defra spokesperson.
Article Summary: 2,500 farmers across England applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using the craft that dates back to thousands of year. Laying the branches down invigorates growth at the point where they have been cut, filling gaps in the hedges.

Article Title: 9-year-old boy spent his father’s $118,000 on YouTube ads promoting his Minecraft and Roblox videos
Article Text:
How a 9-year-old spent $118,000 promoting YouTube videos

The advertising spending continued for three weeks

His father’s company discovered the charges

Mike reportedly thought more spending meant more views

The family may pause Mighty Mike Plays

A nine-year-old boy who runs the YouTube channel Mighty Mike Plays allegedly spent about $118,000 on YouTube advertising to promote his Minecraft and Roblox videos, according to his father, Dave. The situation reportedly began with a much smaller $20 advertising campaign that Dave helped his son create after the boy became frustrated with the number of views his videos were receiving. The company credit card was already saved to the Google account, allowing Mike to launch additional advertising campaigns. Dave said the spending continued for around three weeks before his employer discovered the charges. The boy reportedly believed that spending more money would result in more views for his videos, turning a small promotional experiment into a huge advertising bill.According to Dave, Mike wanted to attract more viewers to his gaming channel and was disappointed that his Minecraft and Roblox videos were not receiving enough attention. His father initially helped him set up a $20 YouTube advertising campaign to promote one of the videos.The campaign was intended to be a small experiment. However, Mike later continued creating advertising campaigns. Dave said his son apparently misunderstood how the advertising budget worked and believed that putting more money behind the videos would generate more views.Because payment information was already available through the Google account, the additional campaigns could reportedly be charged to the saved company card.The advertising reportedly continued for approximately three weeks before the company discovered the charges.During that period, Mike's videos were promoted to YouTube users as advertisements. The promoted content included videos featuring Minecraft and Roblox, the two games that form a major part of the Mighty Mike Plays channel.Dave reportedly said some of the videos received around 200,000 views after being promoted. The increased exposure, however, came at a huge cost compared with the original $20 campaign.The total advertising expenditure was eventually reported by Dave to be approximately $118,000.The situation came to light after Dave's employer noticed the unusual charges on the company credit card.Dave said he was called into a meeting with company management and finance personnel, where the advertising expenditure was discussed. He was reportedly shown the charges accumulated over the previous weeks.The discovery left Dave facing uncertainty about what would happen next. He said he did not know whether the company would ask him to repay the money or what consequences he could face at work.There has been no reported confirmation that Dave has lost his job or that his employer has formally required him to repay the entire amount.The incident appears to have stemmed from a misunderstanding about online advertising rather than an understanding of the enormous financial consequences involved.Dave explained that Mike believed spending more money would lead to more people watching his videos. For a child focused on views, subscribers and gaming content, the connection between advertising expenditure and audience growth may have seemed straightforward.But the advertising system was connected to a company payment method, creating the possibility of charges far beyond the original $20 experiment.After learning about the potential consequences for his father, Mike reportedly said he was "definitely cooked", a reaction that became one of the most widely shared details of the story.The family has discussed pausing the channel while they deal with the situation and reconsider how the account is managed.Dave has said that stronger safeguards will be introduced, including spending limits and parental controls. Removing saved payment information is also expected to prevent a similar situation from happening again.The incident has also drawn attention because viewers had reportedly encountered unusually long Mighty Mike Plays videos being shown as YouTube advertisements. Reports from viewers described lengthy Minecraft and Roblox videos appearing as promotional content.Mighty Mike Plays has built an audience around gaming content, particularly Minecraft and Roblox. The reported advertising campaign appears to have significantly increased the exposure of some videos, but at a cost vastly greater than the original campaign.For the family, the episode began with an attempt to spend $20 to help a nine-year-old get more views. According to his father's account, it ultimately resulted in roughly $118,000 in YouTube advertising charges and an uncertain situation for Dave at work.
Article Summary: Mighty Mike Plays is a gaming channel run by a nine-year-old boy. His father, Dave, helped him set up a $20 advertising campaign to promote one of his videos. The campaign was intended to be a small experiment. However, Mike later continued creating advertising campaigns. He believed spending more money would generate more views. The company credit card was already saved to the Google account, allowing Mike to launch additional campaigns.

Article Title: 'H-1B visas should not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners': JD Vance
Article Text: US Vice President JD Vance has defended the Trump administration’s efforts to reform the H-1B visa programme, saying the system should "not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners."Speaking on the business and technology show All-In Podcast, Vance said the administration pursued changes through executive and administrative measures because of the lack of political support in Congress for legislative reform.“Look, man, we looked at the fraud in the system and we said, you know, one, Congress is not going to pass a law changing this. There just isn't the political will to do it. So what are the things that we can do administratively to ensure that if a tech company is going to try to get an H-1B visa, it's an actual genius,” Vance said.He further said that the programme should focus on workers who can make a substantial contribution to the technology sector and the wider US economy.“It's a person that is going to significantly enrich the tech ecosystem or the American economy. You know, you're not just replacing one accountant who makes $60,000 with a lower-wage foreign accountant who makes $45,000 a year. That is not what the programme exists for,” he added.Vance also highlighted a $100,000 fee introduced by the administration and said officials were examining measures to prevent companies from using H-1B workers while simultaneously laying off American employees.“And so we came up with this idea to impose this $100,000 fee. We're also looking at various ways of preventing companies that use H-1B visas from laying off a bunch of American workers. So you know, one of the things that I find just shocking about this is you'll have a company that applies for an H-1B and they'll say, oh, we're desperate for workers.”He questioned companies that claim they cannot find workers despite having recently carried out large-scale layoffs. “We can't find the workers. And then you go and look at their history and they've laid off 5,000 people. Well, that's ridiculous.”Vance said companies that lay off US workers should not then turn to foreign workers to fill similar positions.“If you're laying off American workers, you shouldn't be going to the market searching for foreign workers to replace them. So we're doing a lot within the confines, of course, of what we're allowed to do legally. We've gotten sued on some of this stuff, but I think fundamentally we're on the right on both the law and the policy,” he added.Reiterating the administration’s stated objective for the H-1B programme, Vance said, “The H-1B should not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners. It should exist to enrich the American economy. And that's exactly what we're trying to make sure it does.”Vance was raised in Middletown, Ohio, and spent summers with extended family in Jackson, Kentucky. His upbringing in Ohio and Appalachia has played a significant role in shaping his political identity.The UP president is married to Usha Chilukuri Vance, an Indian-origin lawyer and former litigator. The couple met at Yale Law School and married in 2014. They have four children.
Article Summary: US Vice President JD Vance has defended the Trump administration’s efforts to reform the H-1B visa programme. He said the system should "not exist to replace American workers with low-wage foreigners" Vance said the administration pursued changes through executive and administrative measures because of the lack of political support in Congress.

Article Title: A teenager who survived childhood cancer started collecting LEGO for the hospital that treated him; his drive has now donated 573 mini-figures and raised $2,575
Article Text: Sometimes a small act of kindness goes so far that it touches your heart for an entire lifetime. Alexander Ackled-Dold still remembers the little things when he was receiving treatment for leukaemia as a child at Southlake's pediatric oncology clinic. The teen recounted how the staff were always kind as he was in and out of hospitals for treatment, they drew smiley faces on his bandages and one volunteer even provided LEGO minifigures to the children whenever they came in for treatment.Now in Grade 12 and cancer-free, he said those actions have made a lifetime of difference and inspired him to do the same for others going through treatment today. “Whenever I would go, I just remembered the little things some of the nurses would do that would make the visit less about me going there to get a treatment,” he said.Thus, Alexander and his family launched the Southlake Superheroes donation drive in September. The campaign sought donations of LEGO figures and cash to donate to Southlake's pediatric oncology clinic. So far, the initiative has donated 573 mini-figures and raised more than $2,575 to help provide new LEGO sets.His father, Simon Ackles-Dold, said the initiative has gone well so far, with the children loving the little figures by all counts."There was good initial feedback, positive feedback," he said. “A lot of the younger kids at Alex’s school were donating their old LEGO figures, so lots of teenagers were giving, which is really nice to see.”The project aims to give kids something fun to look forward to when they receive treatment, akin to what Alexander experienced when he was younger and in that situation. “It’s a good distraction for the kids when they’re there,” Ackles-Dold said.While the campaign does not donate to the children directly, since access is limited during treatment, Alexander said it was great interacting with staff there again, years after he was a patient. “It’s been a long time, and it’s been nice to give back to them and see them all happy about what I’m doing,” he said.The family hopes to be able to grow the effort and continue fundraising in the coming months. They are still collecting cash donations or donations of LEGO figures, though old LEGO sets are disallowed because of the need to sterilise whatever they donate.Interested individuals can donate by contacting the Southlake Heroes Instagram page or GoFundMe page.
Article Summary: Alexander Ackled-Dold was treated for leukaemia as a child at Southlake's pediatric oncology clinic. Now in Grade 12 and cancer-free, he said those actions have made a lifetime of difference and inspired him to do the same for others going through treatment today. His family launched the Southlake Superheroes donation drive in September.

Article Title: Finland's coast is still rising after the Ice Age; around the Gulf of Bothnia, 1,730 acres emerge each year, but waterfront owners may not own the new land
Article Text:
According to the news, Finland’s National Land Survey says the fastest uplift occurs around Kvarken, where the land rises by almost one centimeter a year.

New land does not automatically belong to the nearest owner

The shoreline can move while property boundaries stay put

Owners can seek to acquire the emerging land

A changing coast requires a closer look at the property line

For thousands of years, Finland’s western shoreline has been quietly changing shape. Ground that was once pressed beneath an enormous sheet of ice is still rising, pushing parts of the coast farther out into the Gulf of Bothnia. To the eye, the process can look like nature simply adding more land. For waterfront property owners, however, the reality is more complicated: newly exposed ground does not automatically become an extension of the property behind it. According to an online report by ECONews, during the last ice age, the enormous weight of the Scandinavian ice sheet pushed the land downward by more than 500 meters in parts of the region. When the ice retreated more than 10,000 years ago, the Earth's crust began a slow rebound. The process, known as post-glacial rebound, continues today.According to the news, Finland’s National Land Survey says the fastest uplift occurs around Kvarken, where the land rises by almost one centimeter a year. In southeastern Finland, the rate is less than three millimeters annually. NASA estimates that around the Gulf of Bothnia, about 700 hectares, or roughly 1,730 acres, of land emerges from the water each year.The figure gives a sense of the scale of the transformation, although it does not mean an individual property is gaining land at anything close to that rate. And the National Land Survey estimates that as much as another 100 meters of uplift could still occur near the Gulf of Bothnia.The legal situation becomes particularly interesting when the rising ground appears directly in front of a waterfront property. In Finland, land that was once covered by water but has become dry is known as vesijättö, commonly translated into English as a reliction area. It can form because of land uplift, falling water levels or the gradual overgrowth of waterways. The ownership of that land does not automatically shift to the person whose property happens to sit closest to it. In many cases, ownership remains with whoever owned the original water area. That can mean the newly exposed ground belongs to several property owners collectively through a jointly owned water area, often organized as an osakaskunta. In other words, the landscape can change without the property register changing with it.According to the report, that distinction can have practical consequences. A cottage that once stood directly beside the water may eventually have a stretch of dry land between its boundary and the shoreline. The owner may still have the same property they always had, even though the coast looks very different. Finland’s National Land Survey makes clear that natural changes do not automatically alter property boundaries. The location of the waterline is therefore not, by itself, proof of who owns the ground between a property and the sea. The issue is hardly new. Records from Östhammar, Sweden, describe complaints dating back to 1491, when the retreat of the shoreline had made the town’s old harbor unusable.Waterfront owners are not necessarily left without an option. An eligible property owner can apply to acquire adjacent reliction land through a formal redemption process administered by the National Land Survey. A surveyor assesses whether the land qualifies, determines its value and establishes the compensation to be paid. Once the process is completed, the resulting information is recorded in the property register. The agency estimates that the procedure takes around seven months, although individual cases can take longer. Winter conditions can also delay fieldwork. There are costs involved. Current guidance puts the average procedural cost for a cottage plot at roughly €2,000 to €3,000. That amount covers the procedure itself and does not include compensation to the existing landowner or any applicable taxes.For people living along Finland’s western coast, the lesson is straightforward. A changing shoreline does not necessarily mean a changing property boundary. Before building a dock, extending a yard or carrying out other work on newly exposed ground, property owners need to establish exactly where their legal boundary lies and whether a reliction area exists in front of it. The broader geological story also comes with an important qualification. Rising land is not the same thing as falling sea levels. Future changes along the Gulf of Bothnia will depend partly on how continued land uplift interacts with rising global sea levels.For now, Finland offers a striking example of how slowly moving geology can have very practical consequences. The ice age may be long gone, but its effects are still reshaping the coastline, and creating new questions about where nature ends and property ownership begins.Image Courtesy: ECONews
Article Summary: Land along Finland’s western coast has been rising for thousands of years. But the land does not automatically become an extension of the property behind it. Land that was once covered by water but has become dry is known as vesijättö, commonly translated into English as a reliction area.

Article Title: In 1983, Britain reintroduced a butterfly declared extinct just four years earlier; the large blue has since surged 1,866% and now survives at 33 sites
Article Text:
Why the large blue disappeared

The science behind the comeback

A wider warning from 50 years of records

A butterfly once declared extinct in Britain is now at the centre of one of the country’s most striking conservation success stories. The large blue, which disappeared from Britain in 1979, has been successfully reintroduced and now occurs at 33 sites in south-west England. New figures from the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme show its recorded abundance has risen by 1,866% since 1983. The figures were released by the Joint Nature Conservation Committee (JNCC), alongside analysis from the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH), which marks 50 years of national butterfly monitoring. The recovery stands out against a much more worrying picture for Britain’s butterflies. The UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme has collected more than 44 million records from 782,000 volunteers since monitoring began in 1976. Across 59 native butterfly species monitored over the long term, 33 have declined, while 25 have increased and one has insufficient data. The large blue’s comeback was not simply a matter of releasing butterflies back into the countryside. Its disappearance was linked to a complex relationship between the butterfly, its food plants and a particular species of red ant.The large blue was once found across dozens of sites in England but began disappearing rapidly during the 20th century.By 1950, it occupied only about 25 sites, and by 1972 that number had fallen to just two. It was declared extinct in Britain in 1979. For years, scientists struggled to understand why apparently suitable sites could no longer support the species. Research led by ecologist Jeremy Thomas eventually revealed the hidden link.Large blue caterpillars initially feed on wild thyme. After several weeks, they drop to the ground and are collected by red ants. But the caterpillars can survive only inside nests of one particular species, Myrmica sabuleti, where they spend months feeding on ant grubs before eventually emerging as adult butterflies.The problem was that changes in land management had altered the conditions needed by these ants. Reduced grazing, together with the decline of rabbits, allowed grass and vegetation to grow taller. That changed the temperature at ground level and reduced the areas suitable for Myrmica sabuleti. Without the ants, the butterfly could not complete its life cycle.Once researchers understood the relationship, conservationists could begin rebuilding the butterfly’s habitat rather than simply focusing on the insect itself. Natural England and UKCEH worked on a reintroduction programme using Swedish large blues after experiments showed that the population could adapt to conditions in Britain. The first successful reintroductions followed in the 1980s, with the project expanding across former large blue landscapes in south-west England.Conservation managers restored the short, warm grassland required by the ants through measures including intensive grazing and the control of scrub and trees. Monitoring was used to establish whether the habitat was becoming suitable before butterflies were introduced. The approach eventually produced populations across several landscapes, turning the large blue into an example of how understanding an entire ecosystem can change the outcome for a threatened species.Today, the species survives at 33 sites in south-west England, according to JNCC. Its 1,866% increase since 1983 is the largest rise recorded for any butterfly in the latest UKBMS statistics, although the figure reflects the fact that the species was reintroduced after its extinction in Britain.The large blue’s recovery is also a reminder of what long-term monitoring can reveal. Volunteers participating in the UKBMS have walked more than 1.5 million kilometres while recording butterflies at thousands of sites since 1976. The resulting dataset allows scientists to separate short-term fluctuations from longer changes in butterfly populations.And the broader picture remains concerning. The pearl-bordered fritillary has fallen by 70% since 1976, while the white-letter hairstreak has declined by 80%. The small tortoiseshell has fallen by 87% over the same period. There are other signs that targeted conservation can make a difference. The black hairstreak, for example, has increased by 844% since 1995, while the silver-studded blue has also benefited from intensive conservation work. The latest figures also show why continued monitoring matters. Despite Britain experiencing its sunniest year on record, 2025 ranked only 20th among the 50 years of butterfly monitoring, and no species recorded its best year.For the large blue, however, five decades of research, habitat restoration and monitoring have transformed a story of extinction into one of recovery. Its return shows that when conservation is guided by detailed ecological evidence, restoring a species can mean restoring the intricate relationships that allow it to survive in the first place.
Article Summary: The large blue was once found across dozens of sites in England but began disappearing rapidly during the 20th century. By 1950, it occupied only about 25 sites, and by 1972 that number had fallen to just two. It was declared extinct in Britain in 1979. Today, the species survives at 33 sites in south-west England.

Article Title: ‘Maybe they’ll shoot you’: Carney recalls Trump’s joke on Canada-US ties
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump meets Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in the Oval Office in October 2025

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday shared an ancetedote about his conversation with US President Donald Trump as he pitched Canada as a destination for global investment.Speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday, Carney said his government aims to catalyse C$1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years, targeting sectors including energy, transportation, data, defence and critical minerals."Maybe they'll shoot you," Carney recalled Trump saying, adding that the episode "sort of sums up the relationship that we have."Carney nevertheless described Trump as "a very good host" and thanked him for the gesture. "If we give you a key to Canada, we're not gonna shoot you here. We're gonna welcome you," he said.On the broader relationship, Carney said Canada would remain an important US partner despite the current tensions."We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas," he said. He added that Canada wanted relations based on mutual respect for sovereignty and partnership.The summit brought together investors from nearly 30 countries, with participants managing more than C$100 trillion in assets, according to the Canadian government. Ottawa said the summit generated nearly C$500 billion in new investment commitments.Carney also linked Canada's investment push to a major expansion of its defence capabilities. He said Canada is undertaking its biggest increase in defence spending since the Second World War, with a path to reach 4 percent of GDP in total defence spending by 2030.He added that the country's Defence Industrial Strategy is expected to catalyse C$500 billion in investment over the next decade, including in aerospace, shipbuilding, artificial intelligence, cyber, quantum technologies, robotics and autonomous systems.Carney's outreach comes as relations between Canada and the US remain strained by an escalating trade dispute. The US imposed 50 percent tariffs on some C$20 billion of Canadian goods last month, while Canada introduced retaliatory tariffs on US products in September. Washington has also announced restrictions on imports of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and dairy products that are due to take effect on September 29.At the same time, Carney's government is seeking to diversify Canada's trade and investment relationships, including through closer economic and security ties with the European Union. Canada is also looking to attract investment into energy, mining, technology, infrastructure and defence as it seeks to strengthen its economy amid the ongoing dispute with Washington.
Article Summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government aims to catalyse C$1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years. Carney described Trump as "a very good host" and thanked him for the gesture. The outreach comes as relations between Canada and the US remain strained by an escalating trade dispute.

Article Title: Video: 3 killed as helicopter crashes while covering bus collision in LA
Article Text:
The helicopter came down between two commercial buildings, landing on or near several vehicles and shipping containers

Poll Vote & Share your view What is most important for improving air safety? Regular aircraft inspections Proper pilot training Strict safety regulations Better emergency preparedness 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Three people were killed after a Los Angeles news helicopter crashed in the San Fernando Valley on Tuesday while covering a deadly SUV-bus collision, with footage from inside the aircraft capturing the terrifying moments before the crash.The helicopter went down in a parking lot near the 9100 block of N Mason Avenue in Chatsworth, close to the site of an earlier collision in which an SUV slammed into a Metro bus, killing two people and injuring six others.Footage from inside the helicopter showed the aircraft apparently losing control before the recording ended as it crashed. The helicopter came down between two commercial buildings, landing on or near several vehicles and shipping containers. A large fire broke out following the impact.Los Angeles Fire Department Captain Branden Silverman said one person was confirmed dead at the scene. The victim appeared to have been outside the helicopter when it crashed.“We’re trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter,” Silverman said during a news conference, adding that the aircraft was “pretty well destroyed”.Firefighters were forced to search through the wreckage to determine whether there were other people aboard and to identify the aircraft.It was not immediately clear how many people were inside at the time of the crash.Local media reported that the helicopter belonged to a television station, while CBS said the exact station had not immediately been confirmed.The helicopter had been covering the earlier bus crash, in which an SUV was partially lodged inside a Metro bus. Emergency crews were still responding to that scene when the aircraft came down nearby.The Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board have been contacted to assist with the investigation, while Los Angeles police are also investigating the helicopter crash.
Article Summary: The aircraft came down in a parking lot near the 9100 block of N Mason Avenue in Chatsworth, close to the site of an earlier collision in which an SUV slammed into a Metro bus. Footage from inside the helicopter showed the aircraft apparently losing control before the recording ended.

Article Title: Meet Austin Jin, the 16-year-old Great Neck, New York student who built a CRISPR blood test to detect tuberculosis and drug resistance; he won $50,000
Article Text:
Outside the lab, Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter. He also co-founded Project LIFE, a student-led initiative that has grown to over 20 chapters in eight states, with a mission to improve education and access to the bone marrow registry.

Another approach to TB diagnosis

Drug resistance testing

Research to broader impact

Most teenagers go to a pathology office for a blood test. For Austin Jin, it was the launch pad to address one of medicine’s oldest and most enduring problems: diagnosing tuberculosis. A 16-year-old senior at William A. Shine Great Neck South High School in Great Neck, NY, developed M-CATCH, a diagnostic platform based on CRISPR that can detect tuberculosis from blood and identify drug-resistant strains. According to the Davidson Institute website, his work earned him the 2026 Davidson Fellowship and a $50,000 scholarship. Scroll down to read about his journey.Tuberculosis remains a major global health threat with over a million deaths reported annually worldwide. But one of the biggest challenges in fighting the disease comes even before treatment starts: getting an accurate diagnosis. Sputum, the mucus produced deep in the lungs, is used in many standard TB tests. And that creates a particular problem for young children and severely ill or immunocompromised patients, many of whom have difficulty producing a usable sample.But in the online report, Jin’s project takes a different tack.M-CATCH screens the blood serum for circulating bacterial DNA fragments in the blood. The system uses polymerase chain reactions and CRISPR-Cas12a technology to find genetic signatures associated with tuberculosis.This test is not intended to determine whether tuberculosis exists. It can also look for genetic alterations that make the bacteria resistant to certain drugs and that level of detection can come down to a single change in DNA. Jin engineered CRISPR guide RNAs that can distinguish between these tiny genetic differences and combined them with a microfluidics chip that allows multiple reactions to occur at the same time.The result is a multiplex platform that can screen hundreds of reactions for more than one mutation simultaneously. This could eventually make large-scale testing more practical, especially in places where sophisticated laboratories are not readily available.The path to the finished system had its challenges. Designing good CRISPR guide RNAs was particularly tricky because many candidates that looked good on paper did not work as expected in experiments. Jin had spent weeks testing and tweaking them. He’s interested in more than tuberculosis. He plans to major in biomedical engineering and biochemistry to prepare for a career as a physician-scientist, with the hope of translating laboratory research into useful tools for medicine.Outside the lab, Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter. He also co-founded Project LIFE, a student-led initiative that has grown to over 20 chapters in eight states, with a mission to improve education and access to the bone marrow registry.His M-CATCH platform could eventually be adapted to detect other infectious diseases and possibly even cancer, suggesting a future where a small blood sample could reveal far more than a single diagnosis.Images Courtesy: Davidson Institute
Article Summary: Austin Jin, 16, developed M-CATCH, a diagnostic platform based on CRISPR that can detect tuberculosis from blood and identify drug-resistant strains. His work earned him the 2026 Davidson Fellowship and a $50,000 scholarship. Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter.

Article Title: 'Nauseating lie': Houthis deny targeting Mecca; claim strike on Saudi F-15
Article Text:
File photo: Muslim pilgrims circumambulate the Kaaba, Islam's holiest site at the Grand Mosque, during the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Mecca, Saudi Arabia

From Mecca to Jazan: Pressure inside Saudi Arabia

Oil pipeline: A major pressure point

A satellite image shows a closer view of the damage at the Saudi Arabia East-West pipeline, located across the Arabian Peninsula, after a strike that hit it on September 11, 2026, in Saudi Arabia, September 13, 2026. Vantor/Handout via REUTERS

Red Sea: Houthis push towards a strategic chokepoint

Why Riyadh is running out of room

Political exit is getting harder

For the first time ever in the history of the Islamic holy city, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued an emergency alert warning of a possible hostile aerial attack in Mecca.The alert advised residents to move indoors to safe locations and stay away from windows and doors until the danger had passed. Similar warnings were issued for Jeddah and Taif governorates.The alert was lifted within minutes, but it came as Saudi Arabia faces a widening security challenge from the Iran-backed Houthi group, which has intensified attacks on the kingdom while making territorial gains along Yemen’s strategically important Red Sea coast.The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) also condemned what it described as “heinous attacks” by the Houthis against Mecca and the Medina region, saying the attacks threatened civilians, violated the sanctity of holy sites and mosques, and provoked Muslims around the world.The OIC described attacks on holy sites, mosques and civilian infrastructure as terrorism and called such violations “unacceptable and intolerable”. It expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia and backed measures taken by Riyadh to protect its security, sovereignty, civilians and the holy sites.Houthis however have outright denied targeting the holy city of Mecca, with a member of the group's political bureau calling Riyadh's claim a lie.Hizam al-Asad said in a post on X, "The fabrications and lies promoted by the criminal Al Saud regime regarding the targeting of the Honorable Mecca cannot deceive anyone, for it is they who desecrate it with debauchery and licentiousness and by importing prostitutes, and there is no threat from Yemen to the sanctities. Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites. "But Mecca is only the most sensitive point in a much wider problem confronting Riyadh.The latest alert followed a series of attacks and warnings across Saudi Arabia.On September 12, a projectile launched by Yemen’s Houthis landed in the Jazan region, injuring two people and damaging a mosque, several buildings and vehicles, according to Saudi Civil Defence.A day later, the Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen said Houthi forces had attacked civilian areas in Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif using ballistic missiles and drones.Coalition spokesperson Major General Turki Al-Maliki said 13 civilians suffered minor to moderate injuries, while seven residential homes and two vehicles were damaged. Saudi Arabia subsequently warned that it would respond to further attacks.Saudi authorities also issued alerts for Jeddah and Taif on Tuesday, ordering people to move indoors and stay away from windows and doors while the danger remained.The threat is not confined to missiles and drones targeting cities.On September 11, Saudi Arabia shut its 1,200-kilometre East-West oil pipeline after it was targeted in a drone attack launched from Iraq. No group claimed responsibility, while US President Donald Trump blamed Tehran, with Iranian proxies known to operate in Iraq, according to CNN.The pipeline has become particularly important because the war with Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. CNN reported that Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the East-West route to move around 5 million barrels of oil a day that would otherwise have been exported through the Persian Gulf.The attack therefore raised concerns in Riyadh about a wider campaign against critical Saudi infrastructure.CNN reported that Saudi Arabia had already been warned last month about the possibility of “multiple coordinated attacks” involving Iraqi militias working with the Iran-backed Houthis.The pipeline attack was not attributed to the Houthis, but it added to the broader pressure Saudi Arabia faces from Iran-aligned groups operating on multiple fronts.At the same time, the Houthis have been expanding their territorial reach in western Yemen.The group captured the strategic Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea and the port town of Mocha as it sought greater control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping and energy route.Houthi media also reported that the group had captured fighters recruited by Saudi-backed forces who were stationed on the Red Sea islands of Hanish.The Hanish islands lie roughly 160 kilometres north of Bab al-Mandeb, close to routes linking the strait with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.The advances give the Houthis greater strategic depth along a major maritime corridor while putting further pressure on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea interests.Though Saudi Arabia has modern military and greater resources compared to a proxy group, the Houthis have shaped into a threat that needs to be taken seriously.Analysts cited by CNN said Riyadh does not want an all-out war but could increasingly be pushed towards one.Mohammed Al-Basha, a Yemen expert and Washington-based risk adviser, told CNN that signs pointed towards a large-scale Saudi retaliation and that “they don’t have an option”.Cinzia Bianco, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told CNN that a major Saudi escalation could develop into an open-ended conflict similar to Yemen’s previous war.It could also pull Saudi Arabia deeper into the wider US-Iran conflict.That leaves Saudi Arabia looking for outside support while Washington appears reluctant to directly enter another fight.CNN reported that the US has resisted Saudi pressure to become directly involved militarily against the Houthis.Washington has, however, sent around 100 military advisers to Saudi Arabia to provide intelligence for its military campaign, according to multiple sources.US involvement also faces competing pressures, including the ongoing crisis around the Strait of Hormuz and domestic political considerations in Washington.Saudi Arabia has so far shown what analysts describe as “strategic patience”, repeatedly warning and condemning the Houthis and Iran without launching a full-scale retaliation.After the East-West pipeline attack, the Saudi foreign ministry said the kingdom had chosen not to respond at that stage and would support efforts by the Iraqi government, while reserving the right to take measures necessary to protect its sovereignty.But Bianco told CNN that Saudi Arabia had “exhausted the political solutions”.The alternative, negotiating with the Houthis, could also carry a heavy political and strategic cost.Salman Al-Ansari, a Saudi geopolitical analyst, told CNN that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government’s military campaign against the Houthis was already underway and could intensify substantially in the coming days or even hours.He said there could be “major surprises on multiple fronts”.
Article Summary: For the first time ever in the history of the Islamic holy city, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued an emergency alert warning of a possible hostile aerial attack. The alert advised residents to move indoors to safe locations and stay away from windows and doors until the danger had passed. Similar warnings were issued for Jeddah and Taif governorates.

Article Title: At 22, Jayden Williams became Stockbridge’s youngest mayor; 10 months later, the city council removed him after a 10-hour misconduct hearing
Article Text:
Allegations of Financial Mismanagement

Lyft rides, haircuts and movie tickets

Personal clothing and tailoring services

Several restaurant visits and meal charges

Misuse of City Assets and Personnel

Defense Claims Personal Grudge

Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council voted to remove him from office following a 10-hour misconduct hearing focused on his administrative conduct, spending and use of city resources. According to local reports, Williams, now 23, was removed after the council reviewed evidence gathered during a months-long investigation. The council’s decision ended a difficult investigation into Williams’ use of public funds, city property and communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander has taken over as interim mayor while city officials prepare for a special election to fill the vacant position. Atlanta News First reported that the city is preparing a formal resolution declaring the mayor’s seat vacant.The hearing lasted from about 9:00 a.m. until nearly 9:00 p.m. City attorneys and investigators presented evidence about Williams’ handling of public money. A major part of the case involved allegations that Williams repeatedly used city purchasing cards for personal expenses. According to evidence presented during the hearing and reported by WSB-TV, the disputed charges included:Investigators also focused on a $322.92 charge made on Father’s Day at Pandora on the Square in McDonough.According to the city’s investigation documents, Williams originally listed the purchase as gift cards for city staff and later said the items had been given to community members. He also filed a form saying the original receipt was missing. Investigators later obtained the receipt. It showed that the $322.92 was spent on beverages and Father’s Day meals for Williams’ family, according to the evidence presented by the city.Williams defended himself during the hearing, saying he did not intentionally use the city card for personal purchases. He also argued that many of the disputed transactions were connected to official city business. WSB-TV reported that Williams said he reimbursed the city for some of the expenses. When questioned about Stockbridge’s purchasing and ethics policy, Williams testified that he had not read it. He said he had not received a copy when he took office, although he had asked for information about the rules after being elected. WSB-TV reported that Williams also maintained that he had not received proper training on the city’s policies.The investigation also examined Williams’ use of a city-owned vehicle and fuel cards. According to evidence presented during the hearing, Williams had a city vehicle checked out for 183 days between January and June. The city said this accounted for all but nine days of his early time in office. Local reporting also noted that the city’s rules require municipal vehicles to be used for official business or emergencies. Williams disputed the city’s interpretation of his vehicle use. Earlier, he said the vehicle remained available to him but that he was not necessarily using it every day. His attorney also argued that Williams had not received comprehensive training on the city’s vehicle policies. The city also presented evidence that Williams accumulated about $2,600 in fuel expenses using a city card during the same period, according to WSB-TV.The hearing also examined Williams’ communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Evidence presented to the council included text messages exchanged in late November and early December, before Williams took office, as well as additional messages sent in January. Reports said the communications included sexually suggestive messages and allegations involving explicit photographs. Police reviewed the communications but did not bring criminal charges. The student was 18 and therefore legally an adult under Georgia law. However, the city continued to examine the matter as a possible violation of the conduct standards expected of an elected official. Williams has said the communications took place before he became mayor. In a previous statement reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, he said the individual was 18 at the time and had never taken part in the city’s “Mayor for a Day” program. City Attorney Quinton Washington said the council considered the evidence as a whole before deciding to remove Williams. “When taken in concert together, the employee treatment, all of those things were things that they felt like did not uphold the standard that Stockbridge would like to see in its mayor,” Washington said.After the council’s vote, Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander defended the decision, saying officials had a responsibility to protect the city and its residents. “The results of the investigation demanded we act,” Alexander said. Alexander also confirmed that he does not plan to run in the special election to permanently replace Williams.“I have no desire to be mayor,” Alexander said. “For me to run for mayor means giving up my ability to vote, and I would never do that.” Williams and his attorney, Robert Kenner, strongly disagreed with the council’s decision. They argued that council members were biased against the mayor and had already made up their minds before the hearing.Kenner said the decision was not supported by sufficient evidence and accused the council of acting because of a personal dispute with Williams. “What happened tonight was very disappointing,” Kenner said. “I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence. I think it was based on a personal grudge against the mayor.”Kenner said Williams has the right to challenge the council’s decision in court. He indicated that the legal team would consider an appeal in Henry County Superior Court. The proceedings had already faced legal challenges before the final vote. Councilwoman LaKeisha Gantt was barred from participating after a judge found that her previous communications showed bias against Williams. The judge’s decision followed evidence involving messages and other communications between Gantt and people connected to the mayor.Gantt therefore did not take part in the final removal decision, according to CBS Atlanta. The city is now preparing for a special election to choose Williams’ replacement. Atlanta News First reported that officials are working on the formal steps needed to declare the mayor’s seat vacant and begin the election process. Officials are also expected to determine whether Williams will legally be allowed to run again.
Article Summary: Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council voted to remove him from office following a 10-hour misconduct hearing. The council’s decision ended a difficult investigation into Williams’ use of public funds, city property and communications with a high school student.

Article Title: In 2005, New York buried 1.1 million scrap tyres beneath I-87 near Plattsburgh; the discarded rubber helped replace two ageing bridges with a highway
Article Text:
Discarded tyres, pictured for illustration, alongside I-87 in New York | Wikimedia Commons

Discarded tyres, pictured for illustration, alongside I-87 in New York | Wikimedia Commons

The tyres became the fill beneath the road

Shredded scrap tyres can be used as lightweight embankment fill in highway construction, the approach New York used on an I-87 project near Plattsburgh | Wikimedia Commons

New York was also cleaning up tyre stockpiles

About 1.1 million discarded passenger tyres ended up beneath Interstate 87 south of Plattsburgh, New York inside an engineered embankment built after two ageing bridges over an abandoned railroad were removed. The New York State Department of Transportation used shredded tires as fill beneath the reconstructed roadway, and turned a large waste stockpile into part of the highway project. NYSDOT processed tires into large pieces known as tire shreds and used them as lightweight fill in selected embankment projects instead of sending the material to disposal sites. The state’s Tire Shred Initiative was developed alongside the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation as a way to address waste-tire stockpiles while using the material in highway construction.The I-87 project involved two bridges that carried the interstate over the abandoned Delaware and Hudson Railroad in Clinton County, south of Plattsburgh. Engineers removed them and filled the old railroad crossing with tire shreds and conventional earthen embankment material rather than rehabilitating or replacing the bridges. The new fill then supported the reconstructed roadway.NYSDOT’s own account says the tire-shred embankment represented approximately 1.1 million passenger tires and was completed in early 2005.The agency said the approach avoided the expense and labor that was associated with rehabilitating or replacing bridges that were no longer needed. A separate NYSDOT annual report states that work began in September 2004 under a $2.1 million contract, was completed in November 2005 and involved removing the northbound and southbound I-87 bridges over the abandoned railroad. The replacement used tire shreds together with earthen embankment fill.The tyres were shredded to specified sizes and placed in engineered sections. An earlier NYSDOT annual report described the project as a first-of-its-kind construction effort in the agency’s Region 7 and documented the installation of tire cells that contained hundreds of thousands of tires during the construction process. Tire shreds are much lighter than conventional soil and aggregate, which can reduce the load imposed on underlying ground, although the engineering design has to account for factors such as drainage, settlement and the potential for heat buildup in thick tire-shred fills.NYSDOT records say that by November 2005, two projects under the Tire Shred Initiative had used the equivalent of about 1.4 million tires and helped remediate two waste-tire sites. The second project, on State Route 240X in Erie County, used nearly 300,000 tires in a new embankment section. A technical summary prepared for NYSDOT and the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation describes the wider program and its environmental controls, and states that the I-87 Railroad Grade Crossing Elimination Project used approximately 1.1 million tires and was completed in spring 2005. The report also says tire-shred embankments were subject to design criteria that were intended to keep them above the water table and away from environmentally sensitive locations.The state monitored water quality around the projects, with testing for metals and other potential contaminants. The technical report said groundwater testing from the early projects showed very low levels of iron and manganese, while the design guidance took a conservative approach to site selection.NYSDOT had expanded tire-shred construction to several projects across the state by the late 2000s, and its program eventually used millions of passenger-tire equivalents and helped clean up large waste-tire sites. At the Plattsburgh crossing, however, the idea was that two obsolete bridges disappeared, the abandoned railroad corridor was filled, and roughly 1.1 million discarded tires became part of the engineered ground supporting I-87.
Article Summary: Shredded scrap tyres can be used as lightweight embankment fill in highway construction, the approach New York used on an I-87 project near Plattsburgh. The tyres became the fill beneath the road after two ageing bridges over an abandoned railroad were removed. The New York State Department of Transportation processed tires into large pieces known as tire shreds.

Article Title: In 2008, volunteers began turning 6.25 acres of Illinois cornfield into prairie; 15 years later, 134 of 192 planted species remained
Article Text:
PC: Wing-Chi Poon/ Wikipedia

What did 15 years of prairie restoration reveal about Illinois farmland

PC: Peterwchen/ Wikipedia

How did the prairie restoration begin in 2008

Prescribed burns and weed control shaped the prairie’s development

Which species established successfully across different prairie habitats

Which factors affected species establishment over 15 years

A prairie planted on a former cornfield in Illinois has shown how a carefully planned restoration can develop over time. At Nachusa Grasslands, a 6.25-acre field was converted into reconstructed prairie as restoration began in 2008, using seed collected from 176 species suited to dry-mesic, mesic, and wet-mesic habitats. Additional seed was added by hand in 2009 and 2010, bringing the total to 192 species. As per the Grassland Restoration Network, the revisit found 134 of the 192 planted species, or 70%, growing there. The survey also recorded 30 native species that were not part of the original planting, while seven non-native species were found in scattered populations.The 15-year revisit found 134 of the 192 species included in the 2008-2010 seed mixes, which means 70% were still recorded in 2025. Stewards visited the site 15 times from April through late October to track the plants present throughout the growing season. They also found 30 native species that were not purposely included in the original seed mix, along with seven non-native species growing in small, scattered populations. The 2025 survey found 57 planted species with high conservation values, ranging from 8 to 10. Together, these findings indicate that the restored prairie retained many of its original plants while also developing a broader plant community over 15 years.The restoration began after the corn was harvested in 2008. The field was first burned and harrowed, then the seed was divided into three mixes and planted in late November using a drop seeder, with multiple passes to spread it evenly. Each mix was chosen based on the field’s soil type and topography, covering dry-mesic, mesic, and wet-mesic areas. During the 2008 growing season, 225 pounds of bulk seed representing 176 species were collected for the planting. The bulk material included both seed and chaff, with seed accounting for about 40% of its weight.The prairie continued to receive active management after the initial planting. Stewards collected additional seed during the 2009 and 2010 growing seasons and hand-overseeded 99.5 pounds in areas where native plants were particularly sparse. This brought the total number of species in the seed mixes to 192. Once overseeding was complete, prescribed burns were carried out about every other year as part of management of the larger unit. Stewards also monitored the prairie for birdsfoot trefoil, white sweet clover, and reed canary grass. All three became less common over time, although they still required ongoing monitoring and control. Together, additional seeding, prescribed fire and weed management supported the prairie’s development.The 2025 survey found that planted species established at different rates across the prairie’s habitats. About 64% of the upland species were recorded, and 84% of facultative upland and facultative species were recorded. The figures were lower for wetter habitats, with 64% of facultative wet species and 53% of obligate wetland species found. Carex was among the least successful genera, with only three of the eight planted species recorded in 2025. The 30 native species that were not purposely planted also showed different habitat preferences. Thirteen were facultative upland species, while the rest included upland, facultative wet, and obligate wetland plants. These patterns reflected the varied conditions across the restored prairie.The revisit also highlighted why some planted species were not recorded in 2025. The report notes that some may have failed to establish, while others may have lacked the conditions they needed to survive. Certain plants favour limestone soils, while others struggle in richer soil or depend on dry, wet, or sandy conditions. Some species may also emerge only in particular years or remain dormant in the soil as seeds.
Article Summary: A prairie planted on a former cornfield in Illinois has shown how a carefully planned restoration can develop over time. At Nachusa Grasslands, a 6.25-acre field was converted into reconstructed prairie as restoration began in 2008. Additional seed was added by hand in 2009 and 2010, bringing the total to 192 species. The 15-year revisit found 134 of the 192 species included in the 2008-2010 seed mixes, which means 70% were still recorded in 2025.

Article Title: In 1944, SS John Barry sank carrying 3 million Saudi silver riyals; salvors recovered more than 1 million, a 16-ton haul expected to fetch at least $20 million
Article Text:
A Liberty ship similar to SS John Barry, alongside a Saudi silver riyal like those recovered from the 1944 wreck | Wikimedia Commons

A Liberty ship similar to SS John Barry, alongside a Saudi silver riyal like those recovered from the 1944 wreck | Wikimedia Commons

The coins stayed underwater for half a century

Launch of SS Patrick Henry, the first Liberty ship, on 27 September 1941 | Wikimedia Commons​

The wreck remains tied to a second silver mystery

More than 1 million Saudi silver riyals were brought up from the wreck of the SS John Barry in 1994, roughly five decades after the American Liberty ship sank off Oman with 3 million of the coins in its holds. Nearly 16 tons of the recovered silver were headed for a Sotheby’s auction by the following year,, where the lot was expected to fetch at least $20 million.The ship had been carrying the coins to Saudi Arabia during the final years of World War II, and the riyals had been minted in Philadelphia at the request of Saudi Arabia and were intended to help pay workers who were involved in the rapidly developing oil industry. The cargo was kept secret enough that the crew was not aware of the coins, according to the 1995 Associated Press report published by The Christian Science Monitor. The John Barry was torpedoed by a German submarine in November 1944 and sank in the Arabian Sea. Most of its roughly 70 crew members were rescued, while two died. The ship eventually became the target of a specialized recovery operation that involved a modified drilling vessel and equipment that was capable of reaching the wreck on the seabed. The operation reached the cargo hold in late 1994, and the salvors began bringing silver coins to the surface. A detailed account was published by AramcoWorld and records that the salvage operation began in October 1994 by making use of the modified drilling ship Flex LD and a 50-ton video-equipped grab designed by the French research organization IFREMER. The equipment was lowered through more than a mile of water to reach the wreck. In early November, the first silver was identified on the video feed, and over the next five days, about 1.3 million Saudi riyals were recovered, weighing approximately 17 tons.The operation reached only some parts of the wreck and cargo spaces, which left a large quantity of the original shipment underwater. The origin of the recovered coins gave them a historical value beyond the metal itself, and Sotheby’s planned to sell the recovered group as a single lot.The Christian Science Monitor reported in November 1995 that more than 1 million of the recovered coins, which weighed almost 16 tons, were expected to bring at least $20 million. Sotheby’s said the coins were being sold together because of their historical association with the wreck.The coins had been ordered for Saudi Arabia at a time when the kingdom needed currency to pay workers, including those involved in the construction of oil facilities. The shipment was therefore part of the financial infrastructure supporting Saudi Arabia’s emerging oil economy.Another claim that was linked to the wreck concerned a much larger quantity of silver bullion that was allegedly aboard the ship, and the existence and ownership of that bullion became the subject of later salvage disputes. A 2026 federal court opinion that reviewed litigation over the wreck records that the ship sank on August 28, 1944, carrying 3 million U.S.-minted Saudi one-riyal coins. The court record states that the first major salvage expedition in 1994 recovered about 1.4 million of the coins but found no evidence of the separate silver bullion that had been the subject of later claims. The recovered riyals are documented cargo, while the alleged bullion has remained disputed. The court record also shows that salvage rights to the vessel had been awarded in 1989, before the 1994 recovery effort.Heritage Auctions has sold salvaged examples described as Philadelphia-minted Saudi riyals from the wreck. The coins recovered in the 1990s therefore did not disappear into a single historical collection, since some have continued circulating among collectors decades after they were lifted from the seabed.The original cargo, however, remains only partly recovered. The 3 million coins that went down with the John Barry were divided between what was brought to the surface in the 1990s and what remains associated with the wreck. The ship that disappeared beneath the Arabian Sea in 1944 still has a portion of its wartime cargo on the seabed.
Article Summary: The John Barry was torpedoed by a German submarine in November 1944 and sank in the Arabian Sea. The ship had been carrying the coins to Saudi Arabia during the final years of World War II. The coins had been minted in Philadelphia at the request of Saudi Arabia and were intended to help pay workers in the rapidly developing oil industry.

Article Title: In 2020, a New Orleans project began crushing bottles into sand; six years later, it has diverted 12 million pounds of glass to help rebuild shrinking coastal wetlands
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

From discarded bottles to recycled sand

The initiative had diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills (Image Credit: Instagram/ @glassgrrrl)

Why recycled glass matters for Louisiana’s coast

Testing whether glass can help rebuild wetlands

Turning a waste problem into a restoration resource

A bottle tossed away in New Orleans does not necessarily have to end its life in a landfill. A project launched in 2020 is giving discarded glass a second purpose; crushing bottles into sand that can be used in coastal restoration. Glass Half Full, founded by Tulane University students Franziska Trautmann and Max Steitz, has grown from a small backyard operation into a larger recycling programme. In February 2026, Tulane University reported that the initiative had diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills. The project is now turning a common waste stream into material that can support efforts to restore Louisiana’s vulnerable coastline.The idea behind Glass Half Full is relatively simple: collect unwanted glass, crush it and give the resulting material a new use. The organisation accepts glass through residential and commercial pickups as well as drop-off programmes before processing it at its facility. According to Tulane University, the operation can process about two tons of glass per hour, turning the waste into sand and gravel for several industries, with coastal restoration being a major focus.That approach grew from the founders’ frustration with the lack of glass recycling infrastructure in New Orleans. When Trautmann and Steitz started the initiative in 2020, they used a small machine and a grassroots collection model. Community support helped the project expand, eventually moving from its early backyard setup to a larger recycling operation capable of handling much greater volumes. The recycled material now has applications beyond coastal work. Glass Half Full produces sand and gravel that can be used in construction, disaster relief and other projects, while the organisation continues to develop its coastal restoration programme.Louisiana’s coastline faces persistent land loss, making the search for restoration materials an important part of efforts to rebuild vulnerable wetlands. Traditional restoration projects can rely on sediment dredged from the Mississippi River, but researchers are examining whether recycled glass could supplement those materials. In April 2026, Tulane researchers described an ongoing experiment involving four constructed islands in wetlands east of New Orleans. Two sets of islands are being compared; one uses dredged river sand, while the other combines river sand with recycled glass sand produced by Glass Half Full. Researchers are studying how vegetation develops on the different surfaces over time.The experiment reflects a broader research effort known as ReCoast, which brings together scientists from fields including ecology, engineering and coastal science. The programme is investigating how recycled glass sand can be used safely and effectively in coastal restoration, including how plants respond to the material and where it may be most useful.The concept is not simply to replace natural coastal sediment with crushed bottles. Researchers are studying how glass sand can work alongside other materials and biological systems. Recent Tulane research has focused on growing coastal cypress and other plants in recycled glass sand. Researchers found that some wetland plants do not grow well in glass sand alone, leading them to examine mixtures containing nutrient-rich Mississippi River sediment as well as beneficial bacteria and fungi. The aim is to create conditions in which plants can establish themselves and eventually help stabilise newly restored areas. That plant growth is important because restoration is about more than adding material to an eroded shoreline. Once vegetation becomes established, roots can help hold sediment together and create habitat, allowing newly constructed areas to develop into functioning wetland ecosystems.Glass Half Full has already worked with Tulane researchers and other partners on restoration projects. The collaboration has included projects in southeast Louisiana, including work at Big Branch Marsh National Wildlife Refuge and with the Pointe-au-Chien Tribe in areas affected by Hurricane Ida.The project’s growth illustrates how a material traditionally treated as waste can be redirected towards a local environmental need. Instead of discarded bottles travelling to a landfill, they can be collected, processed and transformed into a material that researchers are testing for use in wetlands and other restoration projects. The scale has also changed considerably since 2020. Tulane University reported that Glass Half Full has now diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills, while the organisation continues to process millions of pounds each year. The work does not mean recycled glass can replace every source of sediment or solve Louisiana’s coastal land-loss challenges on its own. Instead, researchers are testing where the material can be useful, how it should be mixed with natural sediment and which plants can establish successfully in it.For New Orleans, however, the premise remains strikingly direct: bottles that once represented a waste problem can be transformed into sand and put back to work. Six years after Glass Half Full began, its millions of pounds of diverted glass are becoming part of a much larger experiment in turning everyday waste into a resource for Louisiana’s changing coastline.
Article Summary: Glass Half Full was founded by Tulane University students Franziska Trautmann and Max Steitz in 2020. Since then, the initiative has diverted more than 12 million pounds of glass from landfills. The recycled material can be used in construction, disaster relief and other projects. Researchers are also testing whether recycled glass can help rebuild wetlands.

Article Title: A Washington couple claims they spent nearly $300,000 to build a home on their family land; after years of permits and studies, the state demands they surrender 44 acres before construction can begin
Article Text:
Pic credit: JHallman

The paperwork that never ended

The 44.2-acre restriction

In 2021, Tyler Chambers, 59, purchased 66 acres in rural Chelan County, Washington, with his wife, Wendy, planning to construct a home. The land they bought seemed perfect: it was zoned residential, had power, PUD water, fibre and paved-road access, with other homes nearby. Everything looked promising for the small-business owner from a farming family. He had plans to build a family home and pole barn, plant some orchard acreage, and dreamt that his children or grandchildren would build on the property later. In five years, he spent nearly $300,000 on regulatory requirements, including wildlife studies and geotechnical reports, according to a report by AgWeb.But then the process became a bureaucratic maze. The county asked for more reports and studies, including assessments of stormwater, spotted owls, golden eagles, deer, shrubsteppe and geotechnical risks. Then the state allegedly asked him to place roughly 44.2 acres, about two-thirds of the property, under a permanent conservation deed restriction as environmental mitigation before he could build his home.Tyler Chambers visited the county planning office before breaking ground. He hired engineers, paid for a surveyor, got a geotechnical report and a soil test. All these cost him about $300,000, including wildlife and environmental studies, according to the account he gave to AgWeb.However, each completed requirement was followed by another.When he started preparing the land in 2021 under what he believed was a green light from the county, neighbours filed complaints about his earthmoving. The county opened an investigation, but the enforcement official signed off on the work. Chambers thought he was cleared to proceed.But the trouble had only begun. The county fired its Community Development Director and hired a replacement. What followed was a stop-work order. Then came a cascade of requests: wildlife studies, spotted owl surveys, golden eagle assessments, stormwater analysis, erosion reports and geotechnical drilling. “At the start, we naively believed if we followed the rules, everything would be fine. We were wrong and terribly misled,” Chambers told the outlet. Each study came at a whopping cost.“They kept requesting more and more. We had to do a geotech report where they drilled all over our land. The specialist drove two-and-a-half hours from Seattle, and he kept scratching his head, asking, ‘Why are you having to do this to build a house?’ All I could tell him was, ‘I don’t know,’” Chambers recalled.In Washington, construction of a small number of single-family homes is generally categorically exempt from the State Environmental Policy Act. However, exemptions can change depending on site conditions, critical-area rules and other exceptions. Washington’s rules exempt up to four attached or detached single-family units, with higher thresholds in some jurisdictions.Tyler Chambers’ proposed home in Chelan County nevertheless became the subject of SEPA-related review. The process was unusually burdensome, but there is no independent evidence that his was the only single-home SEPA review in the county’s history. Now came the most extraordinary requirement. According to Chambers, the regulators asked him to permanently set aside 44.2 acres, which is roughly two-thirds of his 66-acre property, as mitigation.“We were completely shocked. They demanded almost everything we owned, meaning 44 acres of our private property placed in a deed restriction; two-thirds of our land. It was obvious that everything we’d been required to do up to that point was part of a fixed game. I can’t properly describe the emotional damage to my wife, Wendy, and the loss of faith we’ve suffered in our county and state, along with extreme financial and mental stress. We’ve been targeted, and I know we are the only ones in Chelan County’s history ever to do a SEPA for a regular house,” he told the outlet.His consultant, Glen Grette of Grette Associates, reportedly testified before a hearing examiner that mitigation was never intended to be a deed restriction. Nothing in the county’s own rulebook justified such a massive restriction for erosion control on a single-home site. Yet the county dug in.Chambers says this regulatory process was nothing but an attack on his property rights. His broker, Jeff Hallman, also criticised the county’s handling of the case. Neighbours who built homes never faced habitat easements. They simply constructed without these demands. There is even a data centre 10 miles away. “About 10 miles away, Microsoft is building a data centre. Microsoft has moved 500,000 cubic yards of dirt. Tyler’s guessed amount of 1,000 is 1/500th of that, like $2 on a $1,000 bill. So how much land was Microsoft asked to set aside? Substantially less than Tyler. Still think conspiracies aren’t real?” Chambers asks.While the requirements have caused him severe financial trouble, Chambers remains determined to build his dream home. “I’ve learned that if you stay silent or try to appease, your situation only gets worse. I’m a changed man now, and I’m not afraid to speak out against governmental abuse at all levels. One thing is certain: We will build our home on our own land.”
